questions.topic: x86-64 Architecture — Stack Alignment on Call (Stack Alignment)
questions.q: What requirement for stack pointer (RSP) alignment does the System V AMD64 ABI specification impose immediately before executing the call instruction?
questions.hint: Think about how many bytes the stack address must be a multiple of to execute SSE/SIMD instructions.
options: Stack must be aligned on a 16-byte boundary
Stack must be aligned on a 4-byte boundary
Stack alignment is not required
Stack must be aligned on a 64-byte boundary
explanations: Correct! The ABI standard for 64-bit Linux/macOS systems (System V) requires that before calling the `call` instruction, the address in the `RSP` register must be a multiple of 16 bytes. This is necessary for vector instructions (SSE/AVX) to work correctly.
Incorrect. 4-byte alignment was used on older 32-bit architectures.
Incorrect. Stack mis-alignment will cause a crash (General Protection Fault) when executing vectorized code.
Incorrect. 64-byte alignment is required only for some cache lines, but not for function call ABI.

questions.q: What does the return type and second parameter type of function signal from <signal.h> mean?
questions.hint: Analyze the syntax: void (*signal(int sig, void (*func)(int)))(int).
options: Function signal accepts a signal number and a handler pointer, and returns a pointer to the old signal handler
Function signal accepts 2 integers and returns NULL
This is a syntax error because a function cannot return a pointer to another function
This is a declaration of an array of 2 functions
explanations: Correct! Function `signal` accepts signal number `int` and pointer to handler function `void (*func)(int)`. It returns a pointer to the previous handler function of the same type `void (*)(int)`.
Incorrect. The second parameter and return value are function pointers, not simple numbers.
Incorrect. In C, functions can return pointers to other functions.
Incorrect. Array square brackets are absent here.

questions.topic: Passing Arrays — Behavior of sizeof Inside Functions
questions.q: What will printf("%zu", sizeof(arr)) output inside function process(int arr[100]) on a 64-bit system?
questions.hint: What does an array parameter turn into when passed to a function?
options: 8 (pointer size int*, because array decays into pointer)
400 (size of 100 elements of int type at 4 bytes each)
100 (number of elements)
Compilation error
explanations: Correct! When passing an array to a function, size specification `[100]` is ignored by the compiler. Parameter `int arr[100]` turns into a regular pointer `int *arr`. Operator `sizeof(arr)` will return pointer size (8 bytes on 64-bit architecture).
Incorrect. Original array size is lost (Array decay) when passed to function.
Incorrect. `sizeof` returns size in bytes, not element count, and works only with pointer type.
Incorrect. Code is completely valid C.

questions.topic: Evaluation Order — Unspecified Behavior in Arguments
questions.q: In what order by the C standard will functions a(), b(), and c() be called in expression foo(a(), b(), c())?
questions.hint: Does the C standard guarantee evaluation order of function arguments from left to right?
options: Order is unspecified (Unspecified Behavior) — compiler can call them in any order
Strictly left-to-right: a(), then b(), then c()
Strictly right-to-left: c(), then b(), then a()
All three functions are called strictly simultaneously
explanations: Correct! The C standard does not specify evaluation order of function arguments. The compiler can call `a()`, `b()`, `c()` in any order whatsoever. Relying on argument call order is unsafe.
Incorrect. In C (unlike C++17 in some contexts) there is no rule for evaluating arguments left-to-right.
Incorrect. Right-to-left evaluation often occurs due to calling conventions (cdecl), but the standard does not guarantee it.
Incorrect. In C, function calls happen sequentially.

questions.topic: Variadic Functions — float Type Promotion (Default Argument Promotion)
questions.q: Which data type must be specified in va_arg() macro to extract an argument passed as float to a variadic function (...)?
questions.hint: Recall automatic type promotion rules when calling variadic functions.
options: double (since float is automatically promoted to double)
float
float*
long double
explanations: Correct! According to Default Argument Promotion rules, any `float` arguments passed to variadic part `...` are automatically promoted to `double`. They must be extracted via `va_arg(args, double)`.
Incorrect. Attempting to extract `float` via `va_arg(args, float)` leads to undefined behavior (UB).
Incorrect. Pointers were not passed if argument was a simple `float`.
Incorrect. Nothing is automatically promoted to `long double`.

questions.q: Why are inline functions defined in header files (.h) almost always declared as static inline?
questions.hint: What will happen if multiple .c files include one .h file with a regular inline function without static?
options: To avoid linker errors about symbol duplication (Multiple Definition) when including .h file in multiple translation units
To force function to run several times faster
Because without static the inline keyword is forbidden by C99 standard
To make all local variables inside function static
explanations: Correct! In C99, a regular `inline` function requires an external definition. If not made `static`, including the header file in multiple `.c` files will cause the Linker to report a `multiple definition` error. Specifier `static` gives each translation unit its own local copy.
Incorrect. `static` affects scope and linkage, not execution speed.
Incorrect. `inline` without `static` is allowed in C99, but has specific linkage rules.
Incorrect. `static` before function does not make its internal variables static.

questions.q: How does __attribute__((pure)) differ from __attribute__((const)) in GCC/Clang compilers?
questions.hint: Can a pure function read memory via pointers or from global variables?
options: Pure function can read global memory and data via pointers, but cannot modify them; Const function cannot even read global memory
Pure function cannot accept any parameters
Const function can work only with const int data types
There is no difference between these attributes
explanations: Correct! `__attribute__((pure))` indicates that function has no side effects, but its result may depend on global variables or pointer memory. `__attribute__((const))` is even stricter — function depends ONLY on its arguments and does not read memory at all.
Incorrect. Both functions can and should accept parameters.
Incorrect. `const` applies to entire function behavior (pure mathematical function), not specific types.
Incorrect. These are two different levels of restrictions for compiler optimizer.

questions.q: How will a C23 compiler react if a function with [[nodiscard]] attribute is called and the returned value is not used?
questions.hint: Think about the purpose of warning attributes regarding ignoring important results (e.g. error codes or memory pointers).
options: Will generate a Warning that returned value was ignored
Will cause a compilation Error and stop build
Program will crash at runtime (Runtime Error)
Will automatically free returned resource from memory
explanations: Correct! Attribute `[[nodiscard]]` informs compiler that function result cannot be simply discarded. Attempting to call such function as `func();` will cause compiler to issue a Warning.
Incorrect. By default this is a warning, not a compilation error (unless `-Werror` flag is enabled).
Incorrect. Attributes work at compile stage and do not cause runtime crashes directly.
Incorrect. C language does not perform automatic resource cleanup.

questions.q: What does const qualifier in parameter void print_msg(const char *str) guarantee?
questions.hint: Does const protect str variable itself (pointer) or data it points to?
options: Function promises not to modify data (string characters) at passed address
Pointer str is forbidden to redirect to another address inside function body
Function can be called only with constant string literals
Function executes in thread-safe mode
explanations: Correct! Entry `const char *str` means data in memory is read-only. Attempting to modify `str[0] = 'A'` inside function will cause compilation error.
Incorrect. Pointer `str` itself can be changed (e.g. `str++`). To forbid modifying pointer itself, `char * const str` would be required.
Incorrect. Regular non-const `char[]` arrays can also be passed into function.
Incorrect. Qualifier `const` does not provide automatic thread-safety.

questions.topic: Function Pointers — Syntax Simplification via typedef
questions.q: What is main advantage of using typedef when working with function pointers?
questions.hint: Compare void (*func)(int) and alias HandlerFunc.
options: Creates convenient type alias, simplifying code readability and variable or parameter declaration
Automatically allocates memory for function code on heap
Turns called function into inline
Allows passing any number of arguments to function
explanations: Correct! Function pointer syntax in C is complex to read. `typedef void (*Action)(int);` creates readable type `Action`, which can easily be used as `Action cb` instead of cumbersome notation.
Incorrect. `typedef` works only at compile stage and does not allocate memory.
Incorrect. `typedef` has no effect on function inlining.
Incorrect. Function signature and number of parameters remain strictly fixed.

questions.q: What is indirect (mutual) recursion?
questions.hint: Does function call itself directly in its last line?
options: Situation where function A calls function B, and function B in turn calls function A
Calling function via function pointer
Calling function inside infinite loop while(1)
Recursion that saves its data on disk
explanations: Correct! Indirect recursion occurs when call chain is cycled through other functions: `A() -> B() -> A()`. This strictly requires function prototypes before their definition.
Incorrect. Calling via pointer is just calling by address.
Incorrect. Infinite loop is not recursion.
Incorrect. Recursion uses standard call stack in RAM.

questions.topic: Function Parameters — Behavior of VLA Array in Parameter
questions.q: What will happen if dynamic size $n$ is passed to parameter of function `void foo(int n, int arr[n])` and `sizeof(arr)` is measured inside that function?
questions.hint: Recall what array parameters always decay into when passed to function.
options: Pointer size (sizeof(int*)) will be returned, since array parameters always decay to pointers
Real array size $n \times \text{sizeof(int)}$ will be returned
Compilation error will occur
0 will be returned
explanations: Correct! Even if array is declared as VLA in function header `int arr[n]`, in context of function parameters it still decays to regular pointer `int *arr`. Operator `sizeof(arr)` will return pointer size.
Incorrect. Size of VLA array is calculated via `sizeof` at runtime only when array is declared as local variable, not function parameter.
Incorrect. Such syntax is fully valid starting from C99.
Incorrect. `sizeof` for pointer will return 4 or 8 bytes depending on system architecture.

questions.topic: Preprocessor — Function-like Macros and Side Effects
questions.q: What is danger of calling macro `#define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))` as `MAX(x++, y)`?
questions.hint: How many times does argument `a` appear in macro body?
options: Argument x++ may be evaluated twice due to macro text substitution, leading to double increment
Compilation error will occur due to increment inside ternary operator
Macro will not compile with ++ operator
x++ will execute before macro call without side effects
explanations: Correct! Function-like macros work via simple text substitution. Call will expand to `((x++) > (y) ? (x++) : (y))`. If `x > y`, variable `x` will be incremented twice, which is a common mistake.
Incorrect. Code will compile without errors.
Incorrect. Increment operator is completely legal in macro expressions.
Incorrect. Macros do not create a function frame, so argument evaluation occurs as expanded expression executes.

questions.q: With which construct introduced in C11 standard can one implement analogue of function overloading depending on passed argument type?
questions.hint: This construct selects an expression at compile time based on argument type.
options: _Generic
overload
_Match
typeof
explanations: Correct! Keyword `_Generic` matches expression type against a set of types and selects corresponding function or expression at compile stage (e.g. for creating `tgmath.h` macros).
Incorrect. There is no `overload` keyword in C.
Incorrect. Construct `_Match` is absent in C standard.
Incorrect. `typeof` returns expression type (C23/GCC extension), but does not perform overload selection by itself.

questions.q: What does compiler extension `__attribute__((always_inline))` guarantee compared to regular `inline` keyword?
questions.hint: Can regular `inline` be ignored by compiler?
options: Forces compiler to inline function body instead of generating call, ignoring standard optimization heuristics
Forces function to execute only once during entire program execution
Automatically converts function into preprocessor macro
Allocates special processor register for function result
explanations: Correct! Regular `inline` is merely a recommendation to optimizer. Attribute `__attribute__((always_inline))` strictly commands compiler to inline function (if possible), even with optimizations disabled.
Incorrect. Function call count does not change due to this attribute.
Incorrect. Function remains full-fledged C function with type checking, not text macro.
Incorrect. Attribute is not related to register allocation.

questions.topic: Syntax — Passing Function Pointer as Parameter
questions.q: How to correctly declare a function parameter accepting function pointer with signature `int func(double)`?
questions.hint: Remember operator precedence and parentheses around parameter name with asterisk.
options: void process(int (*f)(double))
void process(int *f(double))
void process(function<int(double)> f)
void process(int f(double)*)
explanations: Correct! Entry `int (*f)(double)` declares `f` as pointer to function accepting `double` and returning `int`.
Incorrect. `int *f(double)` declares function `f` returning pointer to `int`.
Incorrect. `std::function` is a template in C++, it does not exist in C.
Incorrect. Syntax `int f(double)*` is invalid.

questions.topic: C23 Standard — Declaring Functions with Empty Parentheses
questions.q: How did interpretation of function declaration with empty parentheses `void func()` change when transitioning to C23 standard?
questions.hint: What did absence of void in function parameters mean previously?
options: In C23 notation func() became strictly equivalent to func(void) (accepts 0 arguments), whereas previously it meant unspecified number of arguments
In C23 empty parentheses were completely forbidden by compiler
Notation func() in C23 came to denote variadic function (...)
No changes occurred — func() always meant exactly 0 arguments
explanations: Correct! Prior to C23, declaration `void func()` meant that function accepted *unspecified* number of arguments in legacy K&R style. In C23 empty parentheses `()` officially became equivalent to `(void)`.
Incorrect. On the contrary, empty parentheses became modern standard for functions without arguments.
Incorrect. Ellipsis `...` is used for variadic functions.
Incorrect. Prior to C23 an important syntactic difference existed between `func()` and `func(void)`.

questions.q: Is returning pointer to string literal from function safe (e.g. `return "Hello";`)?
questions.hint: Where are string literals stored and what is their lifetime?
options: Yes, this is completely safe, because string literals have static storage duration and live for entire program
No, this will cause undefined behavior, because string resides on function stack
No, string will be destroyed immediately upon exiting function
Safe only when called with -O3 flag
explanations: Correct! String literals are placed in read-only data segment (`.rodata`) and have static storage duration. Pointer to literal will remain valid throughout entire program execution.
Incorrect. String literals are not allocated on stack (unlike arrays `char str[] = "Hello";`).
Incorrect. Literals are not destroyed upon returning from function.
Incorrect. Compiler optimization does not affect literal lifetime.

questions.topic: Standard Library — Call Order of atexit()
questions.q: In what order are functions registered via `atexit()` function called upon normal program completion?
questions.hint: Recall principle of call stack operation (LIFO / FIFO).
options: In reverse order of their registration (LIFO — Last In, First Out)
In direct order of their registration (FIFO — First In, First Out)
In random order
In alphabetical order of function names
explanations: Correct! By C standard, functions registered via `atexit()` are called in reverse order of their registration (LIFO stack order). Last registered function will execute first.
Incorrect. FIFO order is not used for `atexit`.
Incorrect. Order is deterministic and strictly specified in standard.
Incorrect. Function names in runtime are unavailable for such sorting.

questions.q: What will happen if function pointer is cast to another function pointer type with mismatching signature and called?
questions.hint: Will arguments in registers and stack alignment match?
options: Undefined Behavior at runtime
Compiler will automatically perform type casting of arguments and results
Function will execute correctly without any risks
Call stack will automatically balance itself
explanations: Correct! Explicit function pointer casting is allowed, but *calling* function through pointer with mismatching signature leads to Undefined Behavior due to violation of Calling Convention.
Incorrect. No automatic runtime argument conversion occurs through mismatched pointer.
Incorrect. This can lead to stack corruption or reading garbage from registers.
Incorrect. Automatic stack balancing does not exist under UB.

questions.q: What is macro `__builtin_expect(exp, c)` (or popular `likely/unlikely` macros) used for in function calling and branching?
questions.hint: How does CPU know which code branch to load into instruction cache in advance?
options: To hint compiler Branch Predictor about most likely condition outcome
To measure function execution time down to clock cycles
To protect function from buffer overflow attacks
To automatically generate performance profile
explanations: Correct! `__builtin_expect` passes information about `if` branch probability to compiler. This allows optimal machine code placement in memory, minimizing CPU pipeline flushes (Branch Misprediction).
Incorrect. Functions like `clock()` or assembly instruction `rdtsc` are used for timing.
Incorrect. This built-in macro is unrelated to overflow protection.
Incorrect. Profiling is performed by gprof/perf tools or using `-pg` flags.

questions.topic: Syntax — return Statement in void Functions
questions.q: Is using an expression in return statement inside void function allowed in C (e.g. `return void_func();`)?
questions.hint: Compare C rules with C++ rules where such expression is allowed.
options: No, in C return statement in void functions strictly must not contain any expressions
Yes, if called function also has void return type
Yes, C compiler will simply ignore expression result
Allowed only when -O2 compilation flag is enabled
explanations: Correct! Unlike C++, C standard (C99–C23) strictly forbids using expressions in `return` statement inside functions with `void` type. Entry `return expression;` will cause compilation error.
Incorrect. Even if expression has type `void`, in C such syntax is impermissible.
Incorrect. Compiler will report constraint violation.
Incorrect. Optimization flags do not alter syntactic language rules.

questions.topic: Function Parameters — const int *p vs int * const p
questions.q: What is difference between parameters `const int *p` and `int * const p` in function header?
questions.hint: Note which side of asterisk keyword const is located on.
options: const int *p forbids modifying value at address, while int * const p forbids modifying address itself in variable p
These entries are completely identical
const int *p is allocated on stack, while int * const p — on heap
int * const p makes function private to module
explanations: Correct! In `const int *p` data is constant (cannot do `*p = 10`). In `int * const p` pointer itself is constant (cannot do `p++` or assign new address to it inside function).
Incorrect. Position of `const` relative to `*` fundamentally changes object of constness.
Incorrect. Both parameters are local variables of stack frame.
Incorrect. Function linkage is regulated by `static` keyword, not `const`.

questions.q: Is recursive call of main() function from itself or other functions allowed by C standard?
questions.hint: Recall if status of main() in C differs from C++ standards.
options: Yes, in C recursive main() call is allowed by standard (unlike C++)
No, calling main() from code is strictly forbidden in all C and C++ standards
Allowed only in C89, but forbidden starting from C99
Calling main() is allowed only via function pointer
explanations: Correct! In C, `main()` function is a regular function, and its explicit or recursive call is completely legal by standard. In C++, recursive `main()` call is strictly forbidden.
Incorrect. Prohibition on calling `main()` exists only in C++ standard, not C.
Incorrect. All C standards (including C99, C11, C23) permit recursive `main()` call.
Incorrect. Function `main()` can be called directly by name.

questions.topic: Data Types — Passing Unions into Functions
questions.q: How are union type objects passed into function parameters by default?
questions.hint: Does passing union by value differ from passing struct?
options: By value via complete copying of union memory bytes
Always by pointer only
Only field initialized last is passed
Unions are forbidden to pass into functions
explanations: Correct! In C `union`, like `struct`, is a composite value. When passed into function without pointer, entire union memory region is copied by value.
Incorrect. To pass by pointer, `union Data *p` must be written explicitly.
Incorrect. Function receives entire union memory whole, regardless of active field.
Incorrect. Passing `union` is fully supported by language.

questions.q: What is macro va_copy(dest, src) from <stdarg.h> library used for?
questions.hint: Think how to repeatedly iterate over variadic arguments inside single function.
options: For duplicating variadic argument traversal state, allowing to iterate over them again
For allocating memory for new arguments on heap
For converting va_list into string format
For passing va_list into another execution thread
explanations: Correct! `va_copy` creates exact copy of `va_list` state. This is necessary if variadic argument list needs to be read multiple times (e.g. first calculate size, then format).
Incorrect. `va_copy` does not deal with dynamic memory allocation.
Incorrect. Formatting is handled by functions of `vprintf` family.
Incorrect. Passing traversal state between threads via `va_copy` is not its purpose.

questions.q: What does __func__ identifier represent inside function body starting from C99 standard?
questions.hint: What type is this variable and what does it contain?
options: Implicit static character array (const char[]) containing name of current function
Pointer to current function itself
Numeric function ID generated by compiler
Preprocessor macro
explanations: Correct! By C99 standard compiler implicitly declares variable `static const char __func__[] = "function_name";` at start of each function, storing function name as string.
Incorrect. `__func__` is character array with name string, not function pointer.
Incorrect. This is string array, not numeric identifier.
Incorrect. `__func__` is a local variable (predefined identifier), not preprocessor macro (unlike `__FILE__` and `__LINE__`).

questions.q: What action does `__attribute__((cleanup(func)))` attribute perform when applied to function local variable?
questions.hint: Analogue of which C++ concept (RAII / destructor) is this attribute?
options: Automatically calls func(&var) when variable var goes out of scope
Zeroes out variable memory upon entering function
Deletes variable from memory immediately after first write
Forbids modifying variable value
explanations: Correct! `cleanup` extension in GCC/Clang registers cleanup function that is automatically called and receives variable address upon exiting current block (analogue of C++ destructors / RAII).
Incorrect. This attribute does not handle memory zeroing.
Incorrect. Variable exists throughout its scope.
Incorrect. `const` is used to forbid modifications.

questions.q: How does equality operator == behave when comparing two function pointers in C?
questions.hint: Are function entry point addresses in memory compared?
options: Returns 1 (true) if both pointers point to same function (same memory address)
Causes compilation error — function pointers cannot be compared
Comparison always returns 0 (false)
Comparison leads to Undefined Behavior at runtime
explanations: Correct! Function pointers in C store instruction addresses in code segment. Comparing them with `==` operator checks if they point to same memory entry point.
Incorrect. Comparing function pointers is completely legal.
Incorrect. If pointers refer to same function or both are `NULL`, comparison returns 1.
Incorrect. Comparing pointers of same type is strictly defined by standard.

questions.topic: Memory Management — alloca() vs VLA in Loops
questions.q: What is fundamental difference between behavior of VLA (variable length arrays) and alloca() when allocating memory inside loop?
questions.hint: When exactly is stack memory freed: upon exiting loop block {} or upon exiting entire function?
options: VLA memory is freed upon exiting current loop block {}, while alloca() frees stack only upon completing entire function
alloca() memory is freed on each iteration, while VLA persists until end of function
VLA allocates memory on heap, while alloca() — on stack
Behavior is identical, difference is only in syntax
explanations: Correct! VLA lifetime is limited to block `{}` (scope) in which it is declared — stack memory is freed at each loop step. Function `alloca()` advances stack pointer until completion of entire function, which inside loop will cause stack overflow (Stack Overflow).
Incorrect. On the contrary: VLA is freed upon block exit, while `alloca()` accumulates until function exit.
Incorrect. Both VLA and `alloca()` use call stack.
Incorrect. Calling `alloca()` in infinite loop will lead to crash, while VLA in same loop will not.

questions.topic: Function Parameters — restrict Qualifier in C99
questions.q: In what case does using restrict qualifier in parameter `void process(int * restrict ptr)` lead to Undefined Behavior?
questions.hint: What promise to compiler does programmer make when specifying restrict?
options: If at runtime same memory region is accessed via another pointer
If NULL is passed into function
If value at address ptr changes inside function
If function is called recursively
explanations: Correct! Qualifier `restrict` is programmer's promise to compiler that object pointed to by `ptr` has no other associated pointers (no aliasing). Violating this promise leads to Undefined Behavior during optimizations.
Incorrect. Passing `NULL` into `restrict` pointer is not forbidden by itself.
Incorrect. Modifying data via `ptr` is standard usage.
Incorrect. Recursive call by itself does not violate `restrict` if pointers refer to different memory regions.
